extracted.intended_audience: Washington Post journalists, reporters, editors and newsroom staff
extracted.subtask_description: Organization-specific editorial, ethical, sourcing, social-media, verification, corrections, diversity and AI standards that guide Washington Post journalists and editors in reporting and publishing. Covers conflict-of-interest rules, fairness/taste, source handling, attribution, fact-checking, corrections, social media and AI use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest or appearance of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: This news organization is pledged to avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance of conflict of interest wherever and whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post has stringent policies that may be more restrictive than private business norms. The goal is to be free of obligation to news sources and special interests; private behavior as well as professional behavior must not bring discredit to the profession or The Post. Disclose business and professional ties of family/household members to department heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay your own way; no gifts or free trips
rubrics_metrics.description: We pay our own way. We accept no gifts from news sources. We accept no free trips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions to the no-gift rule are few and obvious (occasional, innocent meals). Free admissions to events not free to the public are prohibited, except for seats not sold to the public (press box) or critic review tickets. Whenever possible, arrangements should be made to pay for seats.

rubrics_metrics.name: No payment, honoraria or expenses from covered organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not accept payment — either honoraria or expenses — from governments, government-funded organizations, groups of government officials, political groups or organizations that take positions on controversial issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reporter or editor also cannot accept payment from any person, company or organization that he or she covers. Avoid accepting money from individuals, companies, trade associations or organizations that lobby government or otherwise try to influence issues the newspaper covers. Broadcast organizations, educational institutions and many professional organizations usually fall outside this provision unless the reporter or editor is involved in coverage of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disguised gratuities and entanglements
rubrics_metrics.description: No freelance assignments and no honoraria should be accepted that might in any way be interpreted as disguised gratuities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make every reasonable effort to be free of obligation to news sources and special interests; be wary of entanglement with those likely to be subjects of journalistic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid active involvement in partisan causes
rubrics_metrics.description: We avoid active involvement in any partisan causes — politics, community affairs, social action, demonstrations — that could compromise or seem to compromise our ability to report and edit fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relatives' employment or involvement in causes can appear to compromise integrity and must be disclosed to department heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: No story is fair if it omits facts of major importance or significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness includes completeness: include major facts, avoid omission of important information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: No story is fair if it includes essentially irrelevant information at the expense of significant facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness requires relevance; do not clutter or distract readers with irrelevant material that displaces important facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — honesty (no misleading or deceptive reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: No story is fair if it consciously or unconsciously misleads or even deceives the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness includes honesty — leveling with the reader about what is known and what is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — seek and genuinely consider comment
rubrics_metrics.description: No story is fair if it covers individuals or organizations that have not been given the opportunity to address assertions or claims about them made by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness includes diligently seeking comment and taking that comment genuinely into account; give subjects reasonable opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and decency — avoid prurience and unnecessary profanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post respects taste and decency and shall avoid prurience. Avoid profanities and obscenities unless their use is so essential to a story of significance that its meaning is lost without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenities must not be used without approval of the executive or managing editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use warnings for potentially offensive material
rubrics_metrics.description: If editors decide that content containing potentially offensive material has legitimate news value, editors should use visual and/or text warnings about such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: include a warning such as 'Warning: Some images on this site contain graphic images of war' before linking to external material that may offend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the Legal Department if unsure whether a site falls under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and labeling of news vs opinion/analysis/review
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of news columns from the editorial pages is solemn and complete; labels are used to distinguish types of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels defined: Analysis (interpretation of news based on evidence), Perspective (discussion with a point of view, personal narratives), Opinion (columns/blogs in Opinions), Review (professional critic’s assessment). Analysis and perspective may appear in news columns when plainly labeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media must not harm editorial integrity or reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Post journalist’s use of social media must not harm the editorial integrity or journalistic reputation of The Post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activity on social platforms reflects on The Post; journalists should use platforms responsibly and ensure their posts would not make reasonable people question editorial independence or fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advocacy or partisan presentation on social media
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not appropriate to use your social media account to advocate for causes, issues, governmental policies or political or judicial outcomes; avoid curating feeds that suggest partisan points of view on issues The Post covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guidance does not apply to columnists, critics and other opinion journalists posting as part of their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess social posts before publishing — if harmful, don’t post
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you publish a post on social media, ask if it compromises our newsroom’s mission to prioritize fact-finding or would be harmful if associated with The Post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the answer to any of the questions (compromise mission, harm association, offensive content undermines reputation) is yes, don’t post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be civil and respectful on social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Post journalists should be civil on social media and treat people with respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid engaging in disputes with colleagues online; be mindful that tagging someone can bring undue attention and harassment to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reveal internal editorial discussions or proprietary information
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees may not publicly reveal internal discussions or communications concerning editorial issues or proprietary/confidential business information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes verbal and written communications (email, Slack); expect internal editorial communications to remain private unless The Post publishes them for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using affiliation for personal benefit or endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: At all times, Post journalists should avoid using their affiliation with The Post for personal benefit or private gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not appropriate to use social accounts to air personal grievances, endorse products, companies, nonprofits or political figures, or seek favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect journalists from harassment; report threats to Security and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post will work to protect journalists from harassment and sophisticated campaigns; if you receive threatening messages, contact Security and the deputy managing editor for news operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, Security advises not to respond to threats directly; provide screenshots/links and Security will advise. Consult newsroom leadership before a public response; newsroom leaders and standards editors ensure guidelines are followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope — comply with federal, state and local laws (including NLRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: This policy is intended to comply with all federal, state and local laws, including Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act, and will not be applied or enforced in a manner that violates those laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in this policy is intended or will be applied to prohibit employees from engaging in concerted activities protected under federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: National and community interest — widest possible dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is concerned with the national interest and the community interest and believes those interests are best served by the widest possible dissemination of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of national or community interest by officials do not automatically equate with the public interest; exercise independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist’s role — be the stagehand, not the star; don’t misrepresent identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should make every effort to remain in the audience, to be the stagehand rather than the star, to report the news, not to make the news. In gathering news, journalists will not misrepresent their identity or occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not portray yourself as police, physicians or anything other than a journalist; be honorable and prepared to explain public methods used to obtain information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters have primary responsibility for reporting and fact-checking; multilevel editorial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington Post reporters have primary responsibility for reporting, writing and fact-checking their stories; stories are subject to review by one or more editors in a multilevel structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review may include assignment editors, copy editors and senior editors; digital editors oversee presentation, headlines and alerts. Number of editors/review extent varies with complexity, sensitivity and time pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct all errors promptly and transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakes will happen. When they do, we correct the information as soon as possible, and we are transparent about exactly what we got wrong and what is right so the magnitude of the error is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct all errors, no matter how small, and provide contact methods for reporting errors (corrections@washpost.com or phone with section routing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose sources to readers to the maximum possible extent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post is committed to disclosing to its readers the sources of the information in its stories to the maximum possible extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency helps readers know how and where information was obtained; disclosing sources is honest and fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer named sources; press for on-the-record attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Named sources are vastly to be preferred to unnamed sources. Reporters should press to have sources go on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistently pushing sources to identify themselves often succeeds; if sources refuse, consider seeking the information elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be reluctant to grant confidentiality; grant anonymity only when necessary and with editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: When we use an unnamed source, we are asking readers to take an extra step to trust the information. We must be certain the benefit to readers is worth the cost in credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must know the identity of unnamed sources so they can assess appropriateness. Resist sources who demand editors not be told; if editors aren’t told, the information cannot be published. Only in some circumstances will anonymity be granted; such decisions require deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer at least two independent sources for confidential informant-based factual information
rubrics_metrics.description: We prefer at least two sources for factual information in Post stories that depend on confidential informants, and those sources should be independent of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sources with firsthand or direct knowledge; a relevant document can sometimes serve as a second source. Single-source publication only after deliberations involving executive editor, managing editor and department head, depending on reliability and basis for information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain to readers why unnamed sources deserve confidence; avoid vague attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: We must strive to tell our readers as much as we can about why our unnamed sources deserve our confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic attributions like 'sources' or 'informed sources'; instead give readers contextual descriptors (e.g., 'sources familiar with the thinking of defense lawyers...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat sources fairly and quote in context
rubrics_metrics.description: We strive to treat sources fairly by putting statements into context and summarizing arguments in ways that are recognizably fair and accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potentially controversial statements should be quoted in a complete sentence or paragraph when possible and in context; make clear the question being answered when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give subjects reasonable opportunity to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking comment from people who are the subject of a story, we should give them a reasonable opportunity to respond to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means not calling at the last minute before deadline if timing can be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not promise sources a cessation of further reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not promise sources that we will refrain from additional reporting or efforts to verify the information they may give us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should be cautious about making commitments that limit future reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish ad hominem or blind quotations from unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: We should not publish ad hominem quotations from unnamed sources and should avoid blind quotations whose only purpose is to add color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources who want to attack someone should do so in their own names; anonymous ad hominem attacks are disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use pseudonyms or mislead about identities; explain less-than-full names
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not use pseudonyms, and we do not mislead our readers about the identities of people who appear in our stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rare situations when less than a full name is used (e.g., first name only), editors must participate in decisions and we must explain to readers why full names are not used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fool or mislead sources; identify yourself as a Post reporter
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not fool or mislead sources. When identifying ourselves, we say we are reporters for The Post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting should be honorable; be prepared to explain publicly anything done to get a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful attribution and prohibition on plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: We must be truthful about the source of our information. Facts and quotations not produced by our own reporting must be attributed. Attribution of material from other media must be total. Plagiarism is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give credit to other publications that develop exclusive stories worthy of coverage; ensure clear attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what the reporter saw from what came from other sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should be able to distinguish between what the reporter saw and what the reporter obtained from other sources such as wire services, pool reporters, email, websites, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing events or relying on others’ accounts, attribute appropriately so readers know the provenance of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value original reporting and on-scene reporting when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: We place a premium value on original reporting. We expect reporters to see as much as they can of the story they are reporting and to talk to as many participants as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should consider the advantages of reporting from the scene whenever possible to produce richer coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: If not present at scene, make that clear and attribute reconstructed content
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reporter was not present at a scene described in a story, the story should make that clear. Assertions that something actually happened although it was unseen by the reporter should be attributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing statements or exchanges based on recollections, attribute transparently; discuss uncertain applications with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start interviews with presumption of on-the-record and define ground rules
rubrics_metrics.description: We should start virtually all interviews with the presumption that they are on the record and clarify forms of attribution before beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inexperienced sources should clearly understand they are speaking to a reporter; in taped interviews, begin with ground rules on tape when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of on the record, on background, deep background, off the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear definitions: On the record = attributable by name. On background/not for attribution = attributable to a general description. Deep background = information included but not attributed (to be avoided). Off the record = cannot be used for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain these distinctions to sources; be cautious with 'off the record' and ensure mutual understanding. Avoid deep background if possible; do not accept 'off the record' information unless terms are clear and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow sources to change published quotes; limit sharing of drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not allow sources to change what was said in an original interview once a quote is on the record. Sharing full drafts of stories with outside sources prior to publication is against policy except in extremely rare cases with top-editor permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be acceptable to read portions of complex passages to experts for accuracy; but do not permit sources to alter original quotes; consult editors in gray areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek diverse expert sources and expand the pool of voices
rubrics_metrics.description: We must strive always to get a rich variety of voices into our work and avoid dependence on the same academics or public figures for reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for new specialists — especially women, younger people, people of color, unconventional thinkers and people not routinely quoted — and include ordinary citizens affected by events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity as core editorial value
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity is at the core of Washington Post journalism: engaging a variety of voices as interviewees and first-person writers and striving for a staff that reflects a range of backgrounds and life experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek feedback from diverse communities and release an annual report on staff diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and verification when using AI
rubrics_metrics.description: We are transparent about how and when we use AI. We use AI as a tool to support and accelerate work in ways consistent with news judgment and ethical standards; accuracy cannot be assumed and verification is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AI for tasks like suggesting related content, translation, or sifting documents. Journalists and technologists must be involved in vetting, editing and contextualizing AI outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use AI-generated visuals to represent reality without disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: We will not employ AI to generate images, video or visual works that purport to represent reality without disclosing its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visuals that represent reality must not be AI-generated unless use is clearly disclosed to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect intellectual property and involve staff in AI deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: We believe in the value of our intellectual property and will protect the integrity of our work wherever it is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff (journalists and technologists) should be involved in vetting, editing and contextualizing AI products, tools and experiences.
